# Bounds and Algorithms for Alphabetic s and Binary Search Trees

R. Bruno, R. De Prisco, A. De Santis, and U. Vaccaro _Senior Member, IEEE_

**_Abstract_--Alphabetic codes and binary search trees are combinatorial structures that abstract search procedures in ordered sets endowed with probability distributions. In this paper, we design new linear-time algorithms to construct alphabetic codes, and we show that the obtained codes are not too far from being optimal. Moreover, we exploit our results on alphabetic codes to provide new bounds on the average cost of optimal binary search trees. Our results improve on the best-known bounds on the average cost of optimal binary search trees present in the literature.**

**--Key words: Alphabetic codes, searching, variable-length codes, binary search trees, data structures.**

### I. INTRODUCTION

The Theory of Variable-Length s and Search Theory are strongly intertwined. In fact, _any_ search procedure that identifies objects in a given space, by sequentially executing appropriate tests naturally defines a variable-length encoding of elements in the space. To wit, one can encode each possible test outcome with a different symbol of a finite alphabet, and the concatenation of the (encoded) test outcomes, leading to the identification of an object _x_, gives a _bona fide_ encoding of _x_, for any _x_ in the search space.

More specifically, binary alphabetic codes and binary search trees are basic combinatorial structures that naturally arise in Search Theory [2], [3], [15]. In fact, alphabetic codes are _equivalent_ to search procedures (in ordered sets) that operate through comparison queries with binary results, while binary search trees correspond to search procedures that use comparison queries whose outcome is ternary.

Alphabetical codes have been extensively studied in the Information Theory community (see, e.g., [9], [11], [12], [13], [14], [25], [28], [29] and references therein quoted). Equally, binary search trees have been studied in the Computer Science community, because of the important application scenarios where they appear (see, e.g., [18], [21], [22], [26] and references therein quoted). The two survey papers [1], [24] contain many more references.

It is well known that optimal binary alphabetic codes (i.e., with minimum average length) can be constructed in time _O(m_log_m_) [13], where _m_ is the number of codewords, and that optimal binary search trees (again, with minimum possible average path length) can be constructed in time _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) [18], where _n_ is the number of nodes in the tree. Most of the research activity that followed [13] and [18] has concentrated<tbc>

<tbc>on the following issues: constructing close-to-optimal binary alphabetic codes (equivalently, close-to-optimal binary search trees) via _linear-time_ algorithms, and providing explicit upper bounds on the cost (average path length) of the constructed objects. In this paper, we provide novel upper bounds on the cost of optimal binary alphabetic codes and optimal binary search trees. Our bounds improve on the best bounds known in the literature. Our new results are obtained by accurately analyzing novel linear-time construction algorithms.

### II. PRELIMINARIES

Let _S_={_s_<sub>1</sub>_,...,s<sub>m</sub>_} be a set of symbols, ordered according to a given total order relation \(\prec\), that is, for which it holds that \(s_1\prec\cdots\prec s_m\). A binary alphabetical code is an order-preserving mapping \(w:\{s_1,\dots,s_m\}\mapsto\{0,1\}^+\), where the order relation on the set of all binary strings {0,1}<sup>+</sup> is the standard alphabetical order. We denote by _C_ the set of codewords \(C=\{w(s):s\in S\}\), and by \(\phi=(\phi_1,\dots,\phi_m)\) the probability distribution on the symbols in _S_, that is, \(\phi_i\) is the probability of the _i<sup>th</sup>_ symbol _s<sub>i</sub>_. For each \(s_i\in S\) we denote by _w(s<sub>i</sub>_) the codeword associated to _s<sub>i</sub>_, and by \(\ell(w(s_i))\), or simply by \(\ell_i\), the length of _w(s<sub>i</sub>_).

Given an alphabetic code _C_, an order-preserving mapping \(w:s\in\{s_1,\dots,s_m\}\mapsto w(s)\in\{0,1\}^+\), and a probability distribution \(\phi=(\phi_1,\dots,\phi_m)\) on _S_, we denote the average code length of the code _C_ by

\(\mathbb{E}[C]=\sum_{i=1}^m\phi_i\ell_i.\)

In the following sections, we will occasionally see an alphabetic code as a binary tree _T_ where each edge is labeled either by bit 0 or 1, and each leaf of the tree corresponds to a different symbol \(s\in S\). Sometimes, it will be convenient to identify an arbitrary leaf _s<sub>i</sub>_ of the tree _T_ with the probability \(\phi_i\) of the symbol \(s_i\in S\) that is associated to the leaf. The codeword _w(s_) for the symbol \(s\in S\) is equal to the concatenation of all the 0’s and 1’s in the path from the root of _T_ to the leaf associated with _s_. The order-preserving property of alphabetic codes implies that the leaves of _T_, read from the leftmost leaf to the rightmost one, appear in the order \(s_1\prec\cdots\prec s_m\). As said before, alphabetic codes, in their binary tree representation, naturally correspond to a search procedure that makes use of comparison queries with binary outcomes.

Binary search trees represent, in a sense, a generalization of binary trees associated to alphabetic codes, since the former can take into account both successful and unsuccessful searches. More precisely, any comparison-based search algorithm on an ordered list of elements \(x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_n\) can

Let _x_ be an element that we want to seek for in the list. Each internal node represents a comparison operation between _x_ and the content _xi_ of the node. The outcome of the comparison can be either \(x\prec x_i\), _x=xi_ or \(x\succ x_i\) (see Section 6.2 of \[18\]). Thus, the internal nodes correspond to successful searches, and the leaves to the unsuccessful ones. The cost of a binary search tree _T_ is defined as the average number of questions needed to identify an arbitrary input element _x_. More precisely, given a probability distribution \(\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{2n+1})=(p_0,q_1,p_2,\dots,q_n,p_n)\), where the probabilities of successful searches are _q_1_,...,qn_, and _p_0_,...,pn_ are the probabilities of unsuccessful searches, the cost of the binary search tree _T_, for the probability distribution \(\sigma\), is equal to \(\mathbb{E}[T]=\sum_{i=1}^nq_i\ell(q_i)+\sum_{i=0}^np_i\ell(p_i),\) (1) where \(\ell(q_i)\) denotes the level of _qi_ in the tree, i.e., the number of nodes from the root of _T_ to _qi_, whereas \(\ell(p_i)\) is the level of the parent of _pi_ in the tree \[18\]. We stipulate that the level of the root of _T_ is equal to 1. Note that when the probabilities of successful searches, _q_1_,...,qn_, are all 0’s, the problem of finding an optimal binary search tree for the probability distribution \(\sigma\) is equivalent to the problem of finding an optimal alphabetic code for the probability distribution \(\phi=(p_0,\dots,p_n)\). ## III. OUR CONTRIBUTIONS IN PERSPECTIVE Alphabetic codes have been extensively studied. In this section, we limit ourselves to discussing the work that is most closely related to our findings. We will present our results in Section IV and Section V. In their classic paper \[9\], Gilbert and Moore designed a _O(m_3) time dynamic programming algorithm for the construction of optimal alphabetic codes (that is, of minimum average length), where _m_ is the number of symbols. Hu and Tucker \[13\] improved Gilbert and Moore’s result by providing an algorithm of time complexity _O(m_log_m_). Subsequent studies have mostly concentrated on the problem of giving linear time algorithms for the construction of almost optimal alphabetic codes and in providing explicit upper bounds on the average length of the constructed codes. It is clear that the derived bounds are upper bounds on the length of optimal alphabetic codes, as well. Gilbert and Moore \[9\] gave a linear time algorithm to construct an alphabetic code for a set of symbols _S_, with associated probability distribution \(\phi\), whose average length is less than \(H(\phi)+2\). Here, \(H(\phi)=-\sum_{i=1}^m\phi_ilog\phi_i\) is the Shannon entropy of the distribution \(\phi\). Since the average length of any alphabetic code is lower bounded by \(H(\phi)\), one gets that Gilbert and Moore’s codes are at most two bits away from the optimum. We note that Gilbert and Moore’s upper bound cannot be improved, unless one has some additional information on the probability distribution \(\phi\). In fact, one can see that the average length of the best alphabetical code for a set of three symbols \(s_1\prec s_2\prec s_3\), with probability distribution \(\phi=(\epsilon,1-2\epsilon,\epsilon)\), is equal to \(2-\epsilon\). On the other hand, \(H(\phi)\) can be arbitrarily small. Remarkably, the average length of the Huffman code for the same \(\phi=(\epsilon,1-2\epsilon,\epsilon)\) is equal to \(1+2\epsilon\), thus there can be a difference of (approximatively) 1 bit between the average length of the best alphabetical code and that of the Huffman code, for the same \(\phi\). The general characterization of the "shape" of worst-case probability distributions for alphabetical codes is given in the paper \[16\]. Horibe \[12\] provided a better upper bound than the \(H(\phi)+2\) bound of Gilbert and Moore, by giving an algorithm to construct alphabetic codes of average length less than \(H(\phi)+2-(m+2)\phi_{min},\) (2) where \(\phi_{min}\) is the smallest probability of \(\phi\). Nakatsu \[25\] claimed a different upper bound on the minimum average length of alphabetical codes. Successively, Sheinwald \[28\] pointed out a gap in the analysis carried out in \[25\]. Yeung \[29\] also improved the \(H(\phi)+2\) bound of Gilbert and Moore, by proving the following upper bound on the average length _L_min of optimal binary alphabetic codes: \(L_{min}\le H(\phi)+2-\phi_1\left(2-log\phi_1-\lceil-log\phi_1\rceil\right)\)
\(-\phi_m\left(2-log\phi_m-\lceil-log\phi_m\rceil\right)\) (3) \(\le H(\phi)+2-\phi_1-\phi_m,\) (4) where \(\phi_1\) and \(\phi_m\) are the probabilities of the first and the last symbol of the ordered set of symbols _S_, respectively. In general, the bounds (2) and (3) are not comparable, in the sense that there are probability distributions \(\phi\) for which (2) is better than (3), and probability distributions \(\phi\) for which the opposite holds. A new upper bound on the average length of optimal alphabetic codes was recently given by Dagan _et al._ \[4\]. Their bound claims that \(L_{min}\le H(\phi)+2-\left(\phi_1+\phi_m+\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}min(\phi_i,\phi_{i+1})\right)\) (5) \(=H(\phi)+1-\frac{\phi_1+\phi_m}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}|\phi_i-\phi_{i+1}|.\) (6) While the upper bound (5) is correct, in Remark 1 (which will be given in Section IV) we point out an unresolved issue in the analysis given in \[4\] that leads to (5). Our results for alphabetic codes consist of a series of improvements to the upper bound (5) of Dagan _et al._ on the average length of optimal alphabetic codes _L_min. For instance, we will prove that \(L_{min}\le H(\phi)+2-\phi_1\left(2-log_2\phi_1-\lceil-log_2\phi_1\rceil\right)\)
\(-\phi_m\left(2-log_2\phi_m-\lceil-log_2\phi_m\rceil\right)\)
\(-\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}min(\phi_i,\phi_{i+1}).\) (7)

More importantly, we design a _O(m_) time algorithm to construct alphabetic codes of average length at most the right- hand side of (7). The _O(m_) time algorithm that we design will be instrumental in deriving the results on binary search trees of Section V. We derive further improvements to (5) in Section IV. In Section V we turn our attention to binary search trees. Binary search trees have been extensively investigated (e.g., \[5\], \[21\], \[22\], \[26\]). Knuth \[17\] gave an _O(n_2) time and _O(n_2) space complexity algorithm to construct an optimum binary search tree, i.e., a binary search tree with minimum cost, as defined in (1). The quadratic complexity of the algorithm designed in \[17\] may be prohibitive in many applications, as Mehlhorn remarked in \[21\]. Therefore, Mehlhorn \[21\] proposed a linear time algorithm to construct a binary search tree for an arbitrary probability distribution \(\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{2n+1})=(p_0,q_1,p_1,q_2,\dots,q_n,p_n),\) where the _pi_’s are probabilities of unsuccessful searches and the _qi_’s are probabilities of successful searches, whose cost is not greater than \(H(\sigma)+1+\sum_{i=0}^np_i.\) (8) De Prisco and De Santis \[5\] proposed a different linear time algorithm for constructing binary search trees and they claimed an upper bound on their cost given by \(H(\sigma)+1-p_0-p_n+p_{max},\) (9) where _p_max is the maximum value among _p_0_,...,pn_. Unfortunately, the bound (9) does not hold in general, as pointed out in \[4\], \[19\]. In Section V we correct the analysis of the algorithm derived in \[5\], and we explicitly estimate the cost of the produced binary search trees. The simplest of our bounds states that the cost E\[_T_\] of the tree _T_ constructed by the algorithm of \[5\] is upper bounded by \(\mathbb{E}[T]\le H(\sigma)+1+\sum_{i=0}^np_i-\big(p_0+p_n+\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}min(p_i,q_{i+1})\)
\(+\sum_{i=1}^nmin(q_i,p_i)+\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}min(p_i,p_{i+1})\big)\)
\(=H(\sigma)+1+\sum_{i=0}^np_i-\big(1-\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\frac{|p_i-q_{i+1}|}{2}\)
\(-\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{|q_i-p_i|}{2}+\sum_{i=0}^np_i-\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\frac{|p_i-p_{i+1}|}{2}\big).\) (10) It is apparent that (10) significantly improves the Melhorn bound (8). We derive additional and better upper bounds than (10) in Section V. Clearly, our results also represent upper limits on the cost of optimal binary search trees. The new bounds on the cost of binary search trees are crucially dependent on the new results on alphabetic codes that we derive in Section IV. ## IV. ON ALPHABETIC CODES We first develop some useful machinery. Given a probability distribution \(\phi=(\phi_1,\dots,\phi_m)\), let us denote with \(\nu=(\nu_1,\dots,\nu_{2m-1})=(\phi_1,0,\phi_2,\dots,0,\phi_m)\) its _partially extended_ distribution, and with \(\nu'=(\nu_1,\dots,\nu_{2m+1})=(0,\phi_1,0,\phi_2,\dots,0,\phi_m,0)\) its _fully extended_ distribution. We also need some auxiliary tools and results from Nakatsu \[25\]. **Definition 1.** \[25\] Let \(L=\langle\ell_1,\dots,\ell_m\rangle\) be a list of positive integers. For a binary fraction _x_ and integer \(i\ge 1\), let the function `trunc` be defined as \(\mathtt{trunc}(i,x)=\frac{\left|2^ix\right|}{2^i}\) (11) that is, `trunc`(_i,x_) is the fraction obtained by considering only the first _i_ bits in the binary representation of _x_. Let \(\alpha_i=min(\ell_{i-1},\ell_i)\), for _i_=2_,...,m_. The recursive function `sum` is defined as \(\mathtt{sum}(L,i)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } \mathtt{trunc}(\alpha_i,\mathtt{sum}(L,i-1))+2^{-\alpha_i} & \text{if}i\ge 2, \\ 0 & \text{if}i=1. \end{array}\right.\) (12) To better comprehend the functions `trunc` and `sum` defined above, let us work out a small numerical example. Let _L_={4,2,3,3} be a list of integers. We have \(\alpha_2=min(4,2)=2\), \(\alpha_3=min(2,3)=2\) and \(\alpha_4=min(3,3)=3\). Now, we can compute the value of `sum` for _L_. By definition `sum`(_L,_1)=0. It holds that \(\mathtt{sum}(L,2)=\mathtt{trunc}(\alpha_2,\mathtt{sum}(L,1))+2^{-\alpha_2}\)
\(=\mathtt{trunc}(2,0)+2^{-2}=2^{-2},\) since `trunc`(2,0) takes the value whose binary expansion is the same of the first 2 bits of the binary representation of 0 (that are all 0’s). Similarly, we have \(\mathtt{sum}(L,3)=\mathtt{trunc}(\alpha_3,\mathtt{sum}(L,2))+2^{-\alpha_3}\)
\(=\mathtt{trunc}(2,2^{-2})+2^{-2}=2^{-2}+2^{-2}=2^{-1},\) since `trunc`(2,2-2) takes the value whose binary expansion is the same of the first 2 bits of the binary representation of \(2^{-2}=\frac{1}{4}\), which correspond to the same value 2-2 since the binary representation of \(\frac{1}{4}\) is \(0\frac{1}{2}+1\frac{1}{4}\). Finally, we have \(\mathtt{sum}(L,4)=\mathtt{trunc}(\alpha_4,\mathtt{sum}(L,3))+2^{-\alpha_4}\)
\(=\mathtt{trunc}(3,2^{-1})+2^{-3}=2^{-1}+2^{-3}.\) Intuitively, when `sum`(_L,i)\<_1, one can see that `sum`(_L,i_) enjoys the property of being the smallest value strictly greater than `sum`(_L,i_-1) that differs from `sum`(_L,i_-1) on at least the \(\alpha_i^{th}\) bit of their binary expansion, where \(\alpha_i=min(\ell_{i-1},\ell_i)\). Thus, by denoting with _wi_ the first \(\ell_i\) bits of the binary expansion of `sum`(_L,i_) and with _w__i_-1 the first \(\ell_{i-1}\) bits of the binary expansion of `sum`(_L,i_-1), the property ensures that _w__i_-1 _comes_ before _wi_ in the standard alphabetic order

<tbc>among binary sequences. Moreover, neither _w<sub>i</sub>_ is a prefix of _w_<sub>_i_-1</sub> nor _w_<sub>_i_-1</sub> is a prefix of _w<sub>i</sub>_.

Nakatsu \[25\] proved the following important result (an equivalent result was independently given by Yeung \[29\]).

**Theorem 1.** _\[25\] Let_ \(L=\langle\ell_1,\dots,\ell_m\rangle\) _be a list of integers, associated with the ordered symbols_ \(s_1\prec\cdots\prec s_m\)_. There exists an alphabetical code for which the codeword assigned to symbol s<sub>i</sub> has length_ \(\ell_i\)_, for each i_=1_,...,m, if and only if_ sum(_L,m)\<_1.

Nakatsu proved the sufficient part of Theorem 1 by showing that the first \(\ell_i\) digits of the binary representation of sum(_L,i_), for _i_=1_,...,m_, (under the hypothesis that sum(_L,m)\<_1) give the alphabetic code for the ordered set of symbols \(s_1\prec\cdots\prec s_m\). In the following Lemma 2 we show that an alphabetic code, whose existence is guaranteed by Theorem 1, can be constructed in time _O(m_). We first need the following technical result, whose proof is given in Appendix A.

**Lemma 1.** _Let_ \(L=\langle\ell_1,\dots,\ell_m\rangle\) _be a list of integers such that_ sum(_L,m)\<_1_, let i, j be integers such that_ \(1\le i<j\le m\)_, and let_ {sum(_L,i),_sum(_L,i_+1)_,...,_sum(_L,j_)} _be a subset of consecutive elements of_ {sum(_L,_1)_,...,_sum(_L,m_)}_. For each k=i,...,j_-1_, let t<sub>k</sub> be the smallest integer s for which the binary expansion of_ sum(_L,k_) _differs from the binary expansion of_ sum(_L,k_+1) _on the s<sup>th</sup> bit, and define_ \(t_{ij}=min_{i\le k<j}t_k\)_. Then, it holds that:_

1) \(t_{ij}=\lceil-log_2(\sum(L,i)\oplus\sum(L,j))\rceil,\) (13)

_where_ \(\sum(L,i)\oplus\sum(L,j)\) _is the numerical value whose binary expansion is the result of the XOR operation between the binary expansions of_ sum(_L,i_) _and_ sum(_L,j), and_<tbc>

2) _there exists an index_ \(z\in\{i,\dots,j-1\}\) _such that_ sum(_L,z)\<_trunc(_t<sub>ij</sub>,_sum(_L,i_))+2<sup>-_t<sub>ij</sub>_</sup> and \(\sum(L,z+1)\ge\text{\textit{trunc}}(t_{ij},\sum(L,i))+2^{-t_{ij}}\).

For completeness, we recall that the XOR \(\sum(L,i)\oplus\sum(L,j)\) is easily computable, in most programming languages, with a single built-in instruction. Armed with Lemma 1, we now prove our constructive result. To avoid overburdening the notation, when the pair of integers (_i,j_) in (13) is clear from the context, we will simply denote _t<sub>ij</sub>_ with _t_.

**Lemma 2.** _Let_ \(L=\langle\ell_1,\dots,\ell_m\rangle\) _be a list of integers, associated with the ordered symbols_ \(s_1\prec\cdots\prec s_m\)_. If_ sum(_L,m)\<_1_, then one can construct in O(m_) _time an alphabetic code C for which the codeword assigned to symbol s<sub>i</sub> has length at most_ \(min(\ell_i,m-1)\)_, for each i_=1_,...,m._

_Proof._ To prove the lemma, we design a _O(m_) time algorithm to construct the binary tree associated with the code _C_, that is, the binary tree whose root-to-leaves paths give the codewords of _C_.

It is useful to recall that Nakatsu \[25, Theorem 1\] showed that the code constructed by taking the first \(\ell_i\) bits of the binary expansion of sum(_L,i_) as the codeword associated to the symbol _s<sub>i</sub>_, for each _i_=1_,...,m_, is alphabetic. Our algorithm constructs the binary code tree by using a _subset_<tbc>

<tbc>of the first \(\ell_i\) bits of the binary expansion of sum(_L,i_), for each _i_=1_,...,m_. The algorithm builds the desired tree in a top-down fashion, proceeding by iterated bisections of the set

\(\mathcal{S}=\{\sum(L,1),\sum(L,2),\dots,\sum(L,m)\}.\) (14)

Initially, the root of the tree is associated to the whole set S. To perform the first bisection, we proceed as follows.

For each _a_=1_,...,m_-1, let _t<sub>a</sub>_ be the smallest integer for which the binary expansions of the pair sum(_L,a_) and sum(_L,a_+1) differ on the \(t_a^{th}\) bit, and let \(t=t_{1m}=min_{1\le a<m}t_a\). From Lemma 1, we have that \(t=\lceil-log_2(\sum(L,1)\oplus\sum(L,m))\rceil\). We now compute the index \(k\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}\) for which it holds that

\(\sum(L,k)<\text{\textit{trunc}}(t,\sum(L,1))+2^{-t}\) (15)

and

\(\sum(L,k+1)\ge\text{\textit{trunc}}(t,\sum(L,1))+2^{-t}.\) (16)

We associate the left child of the root to the subset<tbc>

\(\{\sum(L,1),\dots,\sum(L,k)\},\)

<tbc>and the right child of the root to the subset

\(\{\sum(L,k+1),\dots,\sum(L,m)\}.\)

By 2) of Lemma 1, both {sum(_L,_1)_,...,_sum(_L,k_)} and {sum(_L,k_+1)_,...,_sum(_L,m_)} are non empty. The subset {sum(_L,_1)_,...,_sum(_L,k_)} represents the nodes that are in the left subtree of the root. Moreover, by the definition of the function `trunc` and from (15) and (16), each numerical value \(\sum(\cdot,\cdot)\in\{\sum(L,1),\dots,\sum(L,k)\}\) has a binary expansion with 0 in the _t<sup>th</sup>_ position. Analogously, the subset {sum(_L,k_+1)_,...,_sum(_L,m_)} represents the nodes that are in the right subtree of the root and each value \(\sum(\cdot,\cdot)\in\{\sum(L,k+1),\dots,\sum(L,m)\}\) has a binary expansion with 1 in the _t<sup>th</sup>_ position. The algorithm proceeds recursively on the _left_ subset {sum(_L,_1)_,...,_sum(_L,k_)} and _right_ subset {sum(_L,k_+1)_,...,_sum(_L,m_)}. It stops when the cardinality of the subset is equal to 1, in such a case we have just a leaf, or when it is equal to 2, where we have a final subtree with two sibling leaves. The complete pseudo-code of the algorithm is presented in **Algorithm 2**.

The procedure presented above for the construction of the binary tree can be implemented to work in _O(m_) time and space, by exploiting a technique devised in \[7\]. In fact, the crucial operation in Line 9 of Algorithm 1 can be implemented in _O_(logmin(_s,j-s_)) time, where _s=k-i_+1, by first checking if sum(_L,r)\<_trunc(_t,_sum(_L,i_))+2<sup>-_t_</sup> with \(r=\lceil(j-1+i)/2\rceil\) to discover whether the index _k_ belongs to {_i,...,r_-1} or to {_r,...,j_-1}. Therefore, by denoting with _T(m_) the number of operations performed by the algorithm to construct the tree with _m_ leaves, because of Line 9, 10, and 11, we have that \(T(m)\le max_{1\le k\le m-1}\{T(m-k)+T(k)+\alpha log_2min(k,m-k)+\beta\}\)

## V. ON BINARY SEARCH TREES

In this section, we exploit the results on alphabetic codes we have derived in Section IV to provide new bounds on the average cost of optimal binary search trees. We recall that Knuth’s algorithm \[17\] to construct an optimum binary search tree has quadratic time and space complexity; here we provide a linear-time algorithm and give upper bounds on the cost of the trees our algorithm produces. It is clear that our upper bounds apply to optimal trees as well; we will also see that our bounds improve on the best previous results. Since our algorithms to construct almost-optimal search trees take in input almost-optimal alphabetic trees, in order to get linear time complexity it is essential that we can construct almost- optimal alphabetic trees in linear time as well. This is one of the main reasons why we have stressed this feature of the algorithms presented in Section IV.

We start this section by amending the analysis of the algorithm presented by De Prisco and De Santis \[5\] (actually, our presentation is slightly more general than that of \[5\]).

**Theorem 5.** _Let_ \(\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{2n+1})=(p_0,q_1,p_1,\dots,q_n,p_n)\) _be a probability distribution that contains the probabilities q_<sub>1</sub>_,...,q<sub>n</sub> and p_<sub>0</sub>_,...,p<sub>n</sub> for successful and unsuccessful searches, respectively, on an ordered sequence_ \(x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_n\)_. Let C be any alphabetic code for_ \(\sigma\)_, of average length_ E\[_C_\]_. Then, one can construct in linear time a binary search tree T for_ \(\sigma\) _of cost_

\(\mathbb{E}[T]\le\mathbb{E}[C]-\sum_{i=1}^nq_i-\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}min(p_i,p_{i+1}).\) (36)

_Proof._ Let us start from the binary tree _B_ corresponding to the alphabetic code _C_. The tree _B_ has 2_n_+1 leaves,<tbc>

We transform the leaves corresponding to the _q<sub>i</sub>_’s into _internal_ nodes. As in \[5\], we raise each _q<sub>i</sub>_ to the lowest common ancestor of _p_<sub>_i_-1</sub> and _p<sub>i</sub>_, which is at least two levels above _q<sub>i</sub>_. Hence, \(\ell(q_i)\), i.e. the number of nodes from the root to _q<sub>i</sub>_, decreases by at least of one unit, for each _i_. In addition, when we bring up _q<sub>i</sub>_ the whole sub-tree whose root is the sibling of _q<sub>i</sub>_ goes up by at least one level. Hence, at least one between _p_<sub>_i_-1</sub> and _p<sub>i</sub>_ goes up one level. <sup>2</sup> Figure 4 provides an example of the described process.

Therefore, in total we bump up leaves whose total probability is at least

\(\sum_{i=1}^nq_i+\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}min(p_i,p_{i+1}).\) (37)

Let us show that the tree _T_, constructed according to the above procedure, is a correct binary search tree for the distribution \(\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{2n+1})=(p_0,q_1,p_1,\dots,q_n,p_n)\).

To that purpose, let us observe that the search property holds in a binary tree if and only if its in-order visit gives the nodes

By the sake of contradiction let us suppose that it is not the case, that is, there exist _q<sub>i</sub>_ and _q<sub>j</sub>_, with _i\<j_, that have been assigned to the same node _x_. Then, _x_ is the lowest common ancestor both of _p_<sub>_i_-1</sub> and _p<sub>i</sub>_, and of _p_<sub>_j_-1</sub> and _p<sub>j</sub>_. This implies that _p_<sub>_i_-1</sub> and _p_<sub>_j_-1</sub> are in the left sub-tree of _x_, while _p<sub>i</sub>_ and _p<sub>j</sub>_ are in the right sub-tree of _x_. This flagrantly contradicts the fact that in the tree _B_, from which we started, the leaves appear in the order _p_<sub>0</sub>_,q_<sub>1</sub>_,p_<sub>1</sub>_,...,q<sub>n</sub>,p<sub>n</sub>_ (i.e., that _B_ represents an alphabetic code).

The manipulation of the _q<sub>i</sub>_’s to transform them from leaves of _B_ to internal nodes of _T_ can be implemented in linear time, as shown in [5].

Finally, we evaluate the cost of the obtained binary search tree _T_. From (37) the cost of _T_ satisfies the inequality

\(\mathbb{E}[T]\le\mathbb{E}[C]-\sum_{i=1}^nq_i-\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}min(p_i,p_{i+1}).\)

By plugging into (36) either formula (20) of Theorem 2, or formula (22) of Theorem 3, or formula (36) of Corollary 4.2 (according to the hypothesis that holds) we get a series of upper bounds on the cost of optimal binary search trees that considerably improve on the bound (8) of [21], as we asserted in Section III. For instance, by using formula (23) of Theorem 3 in formula (36), we get the upper bound

\(H(\sigma)+2-\sigma_1-\sigma_{2n+1}-\sum_{i=1}^{2n}min(\sigma_i,\sigma_{i+1})-\sum_{i=1}^nq_i-\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}min(p_i,p_{i+1}),\) (38)

already mentioned in Section III.

We remark that our upper bounds on the cost of optimal binary search trees are, in fact, upper bounds on the cost of binary search trees constructed by the _linear_ time algorithm outlined in Theorem 5.

It is worth noting that the binary search trees constructed according to Theorem 5 are not too far from being optimal, and this is due to the lower bounds on the cost of _any_ binary search tree given in [6]. For example, the authors of [6] proved that the cost of any binary search tree is lower bounded by

\(H(\sigma)+\sum_{i=1}^nq_i+H(\sigma)log_2(H(\sigma))-(H(\sigma)+1)log_2(H(\sigma)+1).\) (39)

One can see that (38) and (39) are not too far apart. In fact, the difference between the upper bound (38) and the lower bound (39) is smaller than

\(2-\sigma_1-\sigma_{2n+1}-\sum_{i=1}^{2n}min(\sigma_i,\sigma_{i+1})-2\sum_{i=1}^nq_i-\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}min(p_i,p_{i+1})-H(\sigma)log_2(H(\sigma))+(H(\sigma)+1)log_2(H(\sigma)+1)<2+log_2(H(\sigma)+1)+log_2e-\sigma_1-\sigma_{2n+1}-\sum_{i=1}^{2n}min(\sigma_i,\sigma_{i+1})-2\sum_{i=1}^nq_i-\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}min(p_i,p_{i+1}).\) (40)

Additionally, other results in [6] strengthen the lower bound (39) for particular range of values of the entropy _H_ and thus can be used the reduce the gap between the upper bound and lower bound given in (40). Therefore, in situations where the optimal but onerous _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) time algorithm by Knuth [17] cannot be used, our analysis shows that the _O(n_) time algorithm of [5] is a valid alternative. An additional merit of Theorem 5 is that any possibly improved bounds on the average length of alphabetic codes will immediately translate into improved bounds on the cost of binary search trees.
